title: Words for things I see
keyIdea: Everything you see has a name: sock, hat, cup, robin. Things that look alike can still have different names: a cat has four legs like a dog, but it is not a dog. A group word covers many things: apples, bananas and bread are all food. When a grown-up says a more exact word, like robin, use it: a robin is still a bird, and robin tells us which bird.
familyTip: Name things as you go: 'Here is your sock, now your shoe.' When your child says 'doggy' for a cat, say 'It does look like a dog! It is a cat. It says miaow.' Then give a more exact word for something they already name: 'Yes, a bird. It is a robin.' Use the new word again later that day.

visual.caption: Clothes or food? Drag each word, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: name the clothes, say which animals are dogs, find the group word, learn exact words from Gran, and find things in the park.

kid: Look around you. Each thing has a name. This is a sock. This is a shoe. A sock is soft and goes on first. The shoe goes on top.
A cat has four legs. A dog has four legs too. But a cat is not a dog. A cat says miaow. A dog says woof. A small dog is still a dog.
Some words name a whole group. Sock, hat and coat are all clothes. Apple, bread and banana are all food. We eat food. We wear clothes.
Gran says, "Look! A robin." A robin is a bird. It has a red front. Now you know two words for it: bird, and robin. Robin tells us just which bird.
adult: Ages 3 to 4. Development Matters (2021) asks 3 and 4 year olds to use a wider range of vocabulary, and in Reception to learn new words and use them through the day. The Speaking early learning goal expects children to use recently introduced vocabulary. This lesson covers everyday nouns in simple sets (clothes, food, toys, animals) and the step from a basic word, such as bird, to a more exact one, such as robin.

Young children stretch and shrink words as they learn them. Overextension is using one word too widely: every four-legged animal is a doggy (Clark, 1973). Underextension is using it too narrowly: a tiny dog is not a dog. Both are normal, and both fade when a grown-up names the difference: "It does look like a dog. It is a cat. Listen, miaow."

Common mistakes: calling every animal with four legs a dog; saying a small dog is not a dog; refusing a second name, as in "it's a robin, not a bird" (children first expect one name per thing, the mutual exclusivity bias, Markman 1989); mixing near words such as sock and shoe; and naming one member, such as apple, when the group word, food, is wanted.

Grown-ups help most by naming the exact word for something the child already knows ("Yes, a bird, a robin"), then using it again soon. Children learn many words this way, from talk (Education Endowment Foundation, Preparing for Literacy, 2018). In the lab your child names clothes, sorts dogs from other four-legged animals, finds group words, takes exact words from Gran and uses them to find things in a park.

practice.prompt: It has four legs and says woof. What is it?
practice.hint: Listen for the sound. Which animal says woof?
practice.explain: A dog says woof. A cat says miaow and a cow says moo, though all three have four legs.

practice.prompt: You put on {n} socks and then 1 hat. How many clothes did you put on?
practice.hint: Count the socks, then count on 1 more for the hat.
practice.explain: {n} socks and 1 hat make {=n+1} clothes. Socks and hats are both clothes.

practice.prompt: Ball, teddy, blocks. Which word goes with all three?
practice.hint: What do we do with all three? We play with them.
practice.explain: We play with them, so they are all toys. Ball is just one of them.

practice.prompt: In the park you see {n} ducks and {k} robins. How many birds is that?
practice.hint: Ducks are birds and robins are birds. Count them all.
practice.explain: {n} ducks and {k} robins make {=n+k} birds. A robin is a bird, and so is a duck.

practice.prompt: Gran says, "That is a robin." Is a robin a bird?
choices: Yes, a robin is a bird
practice.hint: Can one thing have two names?
practice.explain: Yes. Bird is the group word, and robin is the exact word for that bird.

pool.prompt: It is soft and goes on your foot first. What is it?
pool.hint: What goes on before your shoe?
pool.explain: A sock goes on first. The shoe goes on over the sock.

pool.prompt: It has four legs and says miaow. Is it a dog?
pool.hint: Which animal says miaow? Is that a dog?
pool.explain: It is a cat. Lots of animals have four legs, but each one has its own name.

pool.prompt: This dog is very small. Is it a dog?
choices: Yes, a small dog is a dog
pool.hint: Does a dog stop being a dog if it is small?
pool.explain: Yes. Big or small, it says woof and it is a dog.

pool.prompt: Apple, banana, bread. Which word goes with all three?
pool.hint: What do we do with all three? We eat them.
pool.explain: We eat them, so they are food. Apple is only one of them.

pool.prompt: Sock, hat, coat. Which word goes with all three?
pool.hint: What do we do with all three? We wear them.
pool.explain: We wear them, so they are clothes. Hat is only one of them.

pool.prompt: You see {n} cats and 1 dog. How many animals is that?
pool.hint: Cats and dogs are both animals. Count them all.

pool.prompt: Dad says, "Find the bird." There are two birds. Which word helps him more?
pool.hint: Which word tells Dad just which bird?
pool.explain: Robin is the exact word. Bird could be either one.

pool.prompt: It has a long arm and a bucket for digging. What is it?
pool.hint: Which one has a long arm to dig with?
pool.explain: A digger digs with its long arm and bucket.

pool.prompt: It has four legs and says moo. What is it?
pool.hint: Listen for the sound. Which animal says moo?
pool.explain: A cow says moo. A sheep says baa and a dog says woof.

pool.prompt: It is a small flower with white petals and a yellow middle. What is it?
pool.hint: Which flower is small and white?
pool.explain: A daisy is small with white petals. A sunflower is big and yellow, and a tulip is a cup shape.

pool.prompt: You name {n} clothes and then you name {k} foods. How many things did you name?
pool.hint: Count the clothes, then count on the foods. Clothes and foods both have names.
pool.explain: {n} clothes and {k} foods make {=n+k} things named. Each one has its own word.
